blocks.prompt: 6 Show that \(\forall\, z_1, z_2 \in C\), \(\overline{z_1 z_2} = \overline{z_1}\,\overline{z_2}\).
blocks.explanation:
This is a proof: it must hold for every pair of complex numbers, so we use letters, not particular numbers.
We must show that the conjugate of a product equals the product of the conjugates.
Plan: write \(z_1 = a + ib\), \(z_2 = c + id\), work out each side separately, and show that they are the same.
steps:
Given: \(z_1, z_2\) are any complex numbers.
To find: prove \(\overline{z_1 z_2} = \overline{z_1}\,\overline{z_2}\).
Method: Write \(z_1 = a + ib\), \(z_2 = c + id\) with \(a, b, c, d\) real. Find the left side (multiply, then conjugate) and the right side (conjugate, then multiply), and compare.

Multiply \(z_1\) and \(z_2\)
\[z_1 z_2 = (a + ib)(c + id)\]
\[= ac + iad + ibc + i^2 bd\]
\[= (ac - bd) + i(ad + bc)\]
Why: Multiply term by term, use \(i^2 = -1\), and group the real and imaginary parts.

Left side: conjugate of the product
\[\overline{z_1 z_2} = (ac - bd) - i(ad + bc)\]
Why: Taking the conjugate changes only the sign of the imaginary part.

Right side: product of the conjugates
\[\overline{z_1} = a - ib, \quad \overline{z_2} = c - id\]
\[\overline{z_1}\,\overline{z_2} = (a - ib)(c - id)\]
\[= ac - iad - ibc + i^2 bd\]
\[= (ac - bd) - i(ad + bc)\]
Why: \((-ib)(-id) = i^2 bd = -bd\); the rest is the same grouping as before.

Compare the two sides
\[\overline{z_1 z_2} = (ac - bd) - i(ad + bc)\]
\[\overline{z_1}\,\overline{z_2} = (ac - bd) - i(ad + bc)\]
Why: Both sides have the same real part and the same imaginary part, so they are equal. Since \(a, b, c, d\) were arbitrary, this holds for all \(z_1, z_2\).

Check with numbers
\[z_1 = 1 + 2i,\; z_2 = 3 - i\]
\[z_1 z_2 = 5 + 5i\]
\[\overline{z_1 z_2} = 5 - 5i\]
\[(1 - 2i)(3 + i) = 5 - 5i \;\checkmark\]
Why: A numerical example agrees (an example alone is not a proof, but it confirms our algebra).
blocks.final_answer: Hence proved: \(\overline{z_1 z_2} = \overline{z_1}\,\overline{z_2}\) for all \(z_1, z_2 \in C\).
